page_intro: I work at the intersection of diplomatic, intellectual, and cultural history, with a focus on the institutions and people who mediated the Cold War divide.

items.title: Cultural Diplomacy & Academic Exchange
items.summary: Cold War public diplomacy, academic mobility, and the institutions that connected the United States with Europe since 1945
items.body:
My work on cultural diplomacy examines how Cold War programs designed to influence societies across the Iron Curtain produced consequences that often exceeded — and sometimes contradicted — the intentions of policymakers. Academic exchange became part of the struggle for influence, but it also created  habits of cooperation and intellectual networks that could not be fully controlled from Washington, Warsaw, or Moscow.

Poland is at the center of this research, viewed within the broader history of East-Central Europe and its changing relationship with Russia. I am particularly interested in what survived the Cold War itself: how exchanges and personal connections formed before 1989 helped shape the region’s post-communist orientation, its relationship with the United States, and the  emergence of a transatlantic political and intellectual community after the collapse of the Soviet bloc.
items.related: Fulbright · public diplomacy · Voice of America · academic mobility · Polish-American relations.

items.title: The Great Alternative: Rethinking East-Central Europe
items.summary: Networks linking Polish émigré political thought with American foreign policy, and changing visions of East-Central Europe during the Cold War and beyond
items.body:
At the center of this research is what I call the “Great Alternative”: the attempt to imagine an East-Central Europe no longer organized around Russian domination or the political order created at Yalta. I trace how this alternative took shape in the dialogue between the Paris-based émigré journal Kultura, one of the most influential centers of postwar Polish political thought, American Sovietology, and policy circles, and how ideas initially developed at the margins of Cold War politics gradually entered broader debates about the future of the region.

Jerzy Giedroyc, the editor of Kultura and a major architect of postwar Polish thinking about East-Central Europe, and Zbigniew Brzezinski, the Polish-born American strategist and Sovietologist who later served as U.S. National Security Advisor, stand at the center of this history. I am currently preparing an edition of their correspondence, but my interest extends beyond their personal relationship to the political world that connected them: understandings of Russia and Ukraine, the nationalities question in the Soviet Union, détente, and the possibility of a post-imperial order in the region. I am especially interested in how ideas that once appeared politically improbable became part of the intellectual vocabulary through which the transformations of 1989–1991 — and their unfinished consequences — were understood.
items.related: Kultura · Sovietology · détente · Brzezinski · Giedroyc · intellectual networks.

items.title: Ukraine, Russia & Imperial Power
items.summary: Ukraine’s place in the Soviet and post-Soviet political order, the contradictions of Soviet federalism, and its central role in Russian conceptions of statehood, empire, and great-power status.
items.body:
My research examines the historical relationship between Ukraine and Russia, focusing on Ukraine’s place within the Soviet system of power and its significance for Russian imperial ambitions. Moving beyond interpretations that reduce this relationship to a rigid opposition between an imperial centre and a subordinated periphery, I explore the contradictions of Soviet federalism, the political agency of Ukrainian elites, and Ukraine’s strategic importance to the Soviet state.

I am particularly interested in how Ukraine shaped Russian understandings of statehood, national identity, and great-power status. The dissolution of the Soviet Union in 1991 marked a fundamental transformation of this relationship, but did not resolve the claims and expectations inherited from the imperial past. My work therefore extends into the post-Soviet period, tracing the contested meanings of sovereignty, the persistence and reinvention of imperial ambitions, and the historical processes that contributed to Russia’s war against Ukraine.
items.related: Ukrainian–Russian relations · Soviet federalism · sovereignty · empire and statehood · political elites · great-power identity · Soviet collapse · post-Soviet relations.
